# UniiChat

▶ Watch the announcement video

This repo is vibe-coded. AI agents wrote nearly all of it, and AI agents reviewed it. Read it, run it and fork it as such: expect bugs.

UniiChat runs a small team of AI agents, the uniis, on a computer you own. You talk to one of them, root. Each unii has one chat that never ends: you talk to the same agent for days, weeks, years, and it remembers. There is no hosted version: you run it yourself, on your own Claude subscription or API keys.

## How it works

- One chat, a memory tree. Every message is summarized into one line, and neighboring lines are merged in pairs, again and again, into a binary tree. Each call sees a view of the whole chat, up to 128 KB: recent messages one line each, older ones covered by fewer, broader lines. Detail fades with age, but nothing is lost.

- Zoom. A unii can open any line into the two it was made from, down to the original message. Its context never rots, and it never needs a compaction that throws the past away.

- Built in the background. Summaries are written as messages arrive. The view changes only at its end, so each call reads most of its input from the vendor's prompt cache.

- A tree of uniis. Root can spawn children, each owning one lasting part of your work (a project, your calendar, your infra), and they can spawn their own. A unii talks only to its parent and its children, by message; a message wakes it, and its turn ends in a reply it keeps for itself. Each works in its own git worktree, and a parent reviews and merges its children's branches. Uniis ask before spawning: nothing grows without your OK.

- Every window is a view. One process, the hub, keeps every chat. A browser tab or a terminal shows them live: the browser lists the uniis as a tree at the left; in the terminal, Tab cycles through them and /tab <name> opens one.

The design is in the header comment of each file. Start with Memory.ts (the tree and the view), Server.ts (the hub) and AskAI.ts (model calls and the cache).

## Run it

You need Bun , git, and Claude Code signed in to your Claude subscription:

git clone https://github.com/VictorTaelin/uniichat cd uniichat bun install claude # sign in, then quit mkdir -p ~/t/unii/root && cd ~/t/unii/root git init && git commit --allow-empty -m root # root's worktree cd - && bun Server.ts # the hub, on http://127.0.0.1:8788

Root works in that repo; each child works in a worktree of it beside it, ~/t/unii/<name> , on a branch of its own. Then, in another terminal:

bun Term.ts # a terminal view

or open the browser view, signed in by the hub's key ( bun Term.ts link prints the same link):

open "http://127.0.0.1:8788/auth?key=$(cat ~/.opt/key)"

The key, ~/.opt/key , is made at the first start; whoever has it reaches every unii and every command they run, so keep it private.

Every unii's chat is a dir chat/<name>/ of the hub's own worktree, ~/t/unii/.chats (branch chats , checked out at chat/ only): one JSON line per message (main/), summary (tree/) and thought (mind/). Only the hub writes them; at the end of each turn it commits that unii's chat, and merges chats into root's branch while root sleeps. They are the memory: back the repo up.

## From your phone, or anywhere

The hub listens only on 127.0.0.1. Run it on a machine that stays on, and reach it over a private network, never the open internet. With Tailscale :

tailscale serve --bg 8788

serves it over HTTPS, at your machine's Tailscale name, to your own computers and phone only. Set site (below) to that address, and open <site>/auth?key=<key> once in each browser.

To let the uniis run commands on another computer (their mac tool), link it to the hub's socket, ~/.opt/mac.sock , with ssh -W : the hub sends {"$":"job","id","unii","command"} and {"$":"stop","id"} , one JSON object a line, and the computer answers each job once with {"$":"out","id","text","code"} (Server.ts says more). Closing the link ends their access.

## Config

~/.opt/config.json (optional). Each key may also be set as the variable OPT_<KEY> :

- root : root's worktree, a git checkout you make (default ~/t/unii/root ). A child's worktree is beside it, ~/t/unii/<name> , on branch <name> , and so is the hub's, .chats .

- chats : the chats' dir in the repo (default chat ).

- site : the address you open it at (default http://127.0.0.1:8788 ).

- vendors : what the uniis may run on, comma-separated: claude-sub (your subscription, through the claude CLI; the default), claude-api ( ANTHROPIC_API_KEY ), openai-api ( OPENAI_API_KEY ).

- models : the models offered: opus-5.5 , gpt-6-astra .

- pick : what a unii runs on until you pick another, vendor:model:effort:speed (default claude-sub:opus-5.5:high:slow ).

- compactor : what writes the summaries (default the same).

- accounts : a dir of claude_<id>.token files, each a token from claude setup-token , used in order: when one reaches its limit, the next. None: the CLI's own login.

- rules : a file appended to every system prompt: who you are, how your files are organized, how you want work done.

- computer : 1 lets the uniis use the screen, mouse and keyboard of the Mac the hub runs on (it compiles Computer.swift with swiftc; macOS asks for Screen Recording and Accessibility).

API keys come from the environment, read at start and removed from it, so no command a unii runs inherits them: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , OPENAI_API_KEY .

Other commands:

bun test # the tests

The hub builds the site's script from web/src as it starts.

# Character.AI export viewer

Open your Character.AI data export and read your characters and chats — in your own browser. The file is read on your device; nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Use it online, free and without an account: amavie.ai/character-ai-export . This repository is the same reader as open source, so you can check what it does with your file or run it yourself.

## What it opens

- Character.AI data export — the ZIP (or the JSON files inside it) from Character.AI's “Export data”: your characters and every chat, with dates and both sides of the conversation.

- Character cards — PNG cards with the card inside (SillyTavern, Chub, JanitorAI, RisuAI, Agnai, Backyard AI) and card JSON.

- Chat exports — SillyTavern .jsonl chats, WhatsApp and Telegram exports, plain text.

## Run it yourself

npm install npm run dev # opens the viewer at http://localhost:5173 npm test # format tests npm run build # static files in dist/ — host them anywhere

Requires Node.js 20 or newer. No server, no analytics, no network requests: the page reads the file with the File API and unzips it with fflate .

## Use the reader in your own code

import { readImportFile } from './src/lib/parse' ; const reading = await readImportFile ( file ) ; // a File from <input type="file"> if ( reading . kind === 'pick' ) { // Character.AI export: reading.pick.characters, reading.pick.chats (messages with role, name, text, time) } else if ( reading . kind === 'request' ) { // one card or one chat: reading.request.card_json, reading.request.chat }

## Where it comes from

The reader is the one Amavie uses to bring a character and a conversation over from another app; src/lib is mirrored from Amavie's codebase, so fixes land there first. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Amavie is a universe of AI characters who remember you and live their own lives — chat with them and play roleplay scenes on the web , iOS and Android.

dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository, packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. When someone allowed asks the agent for work, it opens a work item, works on it in its own agent session and directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example with a pull request. A web panel shows what needs a person.

It is also a way of working with an agent: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. An agent that can act for a whole team can also waste a whole team's attention, so it acts only when asked or when a rule the team wrote allows it, and speaks only when someone must act or can use a result. docs/000-philosophy.md explains the principle and what it asks of the operator.

# AIQuota

See what's left of your AI subscriptions every time you open a terminal.

ChatGPT nearly out until 3 pm? Open Claude instead. AIQuota tells you before you start the coding agent, not halfway through a task.

- A status band when a terminal opens : one section per account, with a green, yellow or red dot showing how close it is to its limit

- In the title bar , always visible and refreshed in the background

- Your accounts, your order : only the ones you list are shown or queried

- Instant : opening a terminal never waits for the network

- Tiny and portable : one POSIX sh script that needs only awk and curl

## Install

List your accounts in the order you want them:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/francescobianco/aiquota/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --display=codex,claude,copilot,freebuff

Then open a new terminal. This installs the script to ~/.local/bin and adds one line to your shell's startup file. To change the accounts or their order, run it again; the line is replaced, not duplicated:

aiquota install --display=claude,codex

Prefer to do it by hand? Put bin/aiquota in your PATH and add this as the last line of your startup file:

## Usage

### The band

● ChatGPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Claude Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Freebuff Free [day 100%]

- The dot is a traffic light for the account's tightest window: green from 50% left, yellow from 20%, red below that. Grey means no data, for example after a login expires.

- [5h 12%] is one window and the share left. An account can have several.

- ↻1h48m is the time until that window resets, shown when less than half is left.

An empty line separates the band from your first prompt. To remove it, add --no-blank-line to aiquota install or to your startup line.

The band always stays on one row. On narrower terminals it gives up detail in this order:

It uses 256 colors where available and falls back to 16 colors and plain ASCII.

### Short names

Add --short-names to aiquota install or to your startup line to always use short names in the band and the title:

● GPT Plus [5h 12% ↻1h48m] [7d 61%] ┃ ● Cld Max 5x [5h 99%] [7d 92%] ┃ ● Fbf Free [day 100%]

The full aiquota view keeps the complete names.

### The title bar

Title bars only show plain text, so this is a shorter summary with no colors or plan names:

ChatGPT 12% 1h48m │ Claude 92% │ Freebuff 100%

For each account you get the share left in the window that will stop you first. The time until it resets appears when less than half is left.

A ~ before a value means it may be out of date: the login expired, the network failed, or the window has reset since the last successful check.

To use it in a tmux status bar:

set -g status-right ' #(aiquota line --plain --display=codex,claude) '

## Accounts

Note

These are mostly undocumented endpoints , the same ones the agents use for their own usage screens. They can change without notice. When one does, AIQuota keeps showing the last known values, marked ~ .

### Flat subscriptions only

This is a deliberate limit, not a missing feature. AIQuota answers one question: which of the agents I already pay for can I still use right now? That means quota measured in time and resources until the next reset. API keys and metered, usage-based plans are never queried or shown, even if they are on your machine.

## Good to know

Logins expire while you're away. AIQuota reads each agent's credentials but never refreshes them, because refresh tokens can rotate and using one could log you out of the agent. So after a long break an account may show login expired , or its last known values marked ~ , until you next open that agent. For example, the Claude access token lasts for hours and the ChatGPT one for days.

It replaces your title. If your title bar normally shows the current directory, that's what you give up. Set AIQUOTA_TITLE=0 before the startup line to keep your title and only get the band when a terminal opens.

IDE terminals show the band, not the title. The band appears each time a terminal opens, in any terminal. JetBrains IDEs use their own fixed tab names, so the title summary doesn't appear there. In VS Code, set "terminal.integrated.tabs.title": "${sequence}" to see it in the tab. In either IDE, run aiquota for the full view.

Gemini is limited by Google. Since June 2026, Gemini CLI login has only been served for Standard and Enterprise seats, so personal accounts show no flat subscription found .

## Settings

Set these as environment variables before the startup line, or in ~/.config/aiquota/config :

## Privacy and security

AIQuota has no server and no telemetry. Each token goes only to the service that issued it.

- Credentials are read-only, and are never copied to the cache or passed on a command line.

- The cache in ~/.cache/aiquota holds only plan names, percentages and times, and only you can read it.

- Text from the network is stripped of control characters before it can reach your terminal.

- Redirects are not followed, so a token can't be forwarded to another host.

## Compatibility

Runs anywhere with a POSIX shell, awk and curl .

## Contributing

New accounts are welcome as long as they are flat subscriptions. See CONTRIBUTING.md .

## License

MIT

# team-solve

A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a Memdoor workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators, solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of GVS5H (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard).

Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a mean of 9.8 of 10 over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone ( below , every run published).

The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method (2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them.

## Five passes on the authors' ten (2026-10-31)

GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model: Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files ( q38_multiagent_pN , fable5_single_pN ), the numbers in their paper. bench/results/parity-5pass/ holds all 50 runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count. 49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused.

Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision. Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown read <scratch> and $HOME ; nothing else in the runs is edited.

Same as the authors'. Every message, byte for byte: lib/test_parity.py runs their multiagent_solve and our workflow against one scripted model and compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker 0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a reply with no text answered by its reasoning.

Different. The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave): 203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their finished steps kept ( log/host-switch.txt ).

What it took. The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2 of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text, top_p / top_k on a model line, mark_cutoff for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on its own four-hour clock.

Where it lost. Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop:

- Pass 5, abc399_e (32 of 44 hidden): round 1's program was right; the manager invented a counterexample with a wrong expected answer, the team rewrote it, and the new program passed the samples, which do not cover the case.

- Pass 4, arc196_c and arc196_d: a program passing every hidden test was overwritten by a later round because the manager did not say done; both got a correct program back before the loop's end (arc196_d at round 8, arc196_c through the final call), at $3.44 and $4.24, the two most expensive runs.

Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the samples). Neither is in these numbers.

## Run it

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash memdoor connect openrouter # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/ # the library: any project sees it mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* . # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait # progress on stderr, exit 0 when every sample passes

/workflow in memdoor tui draws the same run live. For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in / tests/N.out files beside it. The program is solution.py , read from stdin, compared to the samples with diff . It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy the folder into that project's .memdoor/workflows/ . The project's copy wins.

The steps name no model. Whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one included ( memdoor connect local for janis, Ollama or llama-server).

## How it works

plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify └── ideate-b ──┘

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat". The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. There is one repair round and no human gate. The last step is the whole verdict:

type: command requires: - table_pattern: repair command: | check=.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh [ -f "$check" ] || check="$HOME/.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh" bash "$check" > final-test-output.log 2>&1 result=$? cat final-test-output.log exit "$result"

Each step is one YAML file in steps/ , the format of mario , the engine underneath. requires: is the DAG. Changing a role means changing its prompt.

## What the first run found

The sample: count the substrings of a string over {a, b, c} with equal counts of each letter, up to 200,000 characters. Run on the default ladder through OpenRouter:

- 8 of 8 steps, 5 of 5 samples. The solver took ideator A's prefix-state method, O(N) with a dictionary of (a−b, a−c) pairs. A brute force on 300 random strings found no mismatch afterwards, and it runs in 0.04 s at N = 200,000. The manager found nothing to repair.

- One ideator's provider dropped the stream mid-answer. The coder had written max_retries: 0 , so the run died there. The agent steps now carry max_retries: 1 , and the run was resumed with --partition , which kept the planner's and the other ideator's work.

- The ideator prompts the coder wrote named the sample's methods (A: a streaming prefix-state count, B: sorting prefix states), which would steer any other problem the wrong way. They now ask A for the most direct provable algorithm and B for one from a different family of technique (2026-10-28).

- The first attempts failed every step in 0 s with "no agent named coder": a run looked its agent up only in its own workspace. That was fixed in the gateway the same day (v1.692.0).

# bootgpt

A neural network that boots your PC.

The MBR is 512 bytes of hand written asm. It loads an 11.5 KB int8 model from the next 23 sectors and runs it in 16-bit real mode on a 386. No OS, no C runtime, nothing. The machine wakes up and dreams a Linux boot log: timestamps, PCI bars, ACPI events for hardware that never existed.

Build thread: https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757

With 8 chars of context and one hidden layer this is roughly the quality you get:

[ 2.283888] pci 0000:01:01.4: [1b36:0a35] ryndrde c4128 6422 Vveine [ 1.953886] pci 0000:01:1f.2: reg 0x10: [mem 0x7e4515e5-0x2d766c27] usbbore: reg [ 0.206596] Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinu -5.5.2-1-generic gcc version 13.3.0, GNU ld ... [ 1.815765] ACPI: PCI Interrupt Link [LNKA: v/s.xos212 [ 1.883084] NET: Registered protocol family 16

## Run it

brew install nasm qemu python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install numpy ./build.sh ./run.sh

disk.img is a normal boot image. dd it to a USB stick and boot any BIOS box if you have one. It only reads its own sectors.

## Pieces

corpus_gen.py makes 3 MB of fake dmesg. One kernel version and one disk per boot session, because real boot logs repeat themselves and that repetition is what makes a tiny model look sane.

train.py trains the model (char embeddings, one hidden layer, softmax) and quantizes everything to int8 with power-of-two scales, so the boot sector can do the whole forward pass with imul and a single idiv. The script also simulates the exact integer math the asm will run, LCG sampler included, so the Python output and the boot sector output can be diffed. They match char for char.

boot.asm is the entire runtime: int 13h to load weights, int 10h to print, a softclip activation done with cdq/idiv, argmax sampling with timer seeded noise. Any keypress reboots the machine.

record.py records the demo gif from headless QEMU through the monitor socket. No window involved.

The boot sector is code only. Strings, weights and the vocab table all live in the data sectors, it was the only way to fit inference plus BIOS plumbing into 510 bytes.

## Prior art

The boot sector genre is old and glorious. Oscar Toledo put chess , a whole OS and even a BASIC interpreter in there, other people did a C compiler , all inside 512 bytes. His book on boot sector games is a good read.

The closest neighbor is sectorllm , which boots a real llama2 transformer (5 layers, attention, the works) from about 1.2 KB of real mode asm, running Karpathy's stories260K model. sectorlisp-nn runs a TensorFlow-trained network during boot on a Lisp interpreter, and there are UEFI apps that boot straight into llama-class models on modern hardware.

bootgpt takes the other extreme: the whole engine fits in the 510-byte MBR itself, weights and strings live in the following sectors, and the model is not a general story teller but a tiny char-level net trained for exactly one thing, hallucinating the boot log of the machine it wakes up on.

# Context Mode

The other half of the context problem.

Used across teams at

## The Problem

Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides.

### How Context Mode Solves It

Context Mode is an MCP server that solves all four sides of this problem:

- Context Saving — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction.

- Session Continuity — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't --continue , previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate.

- Think in Code — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and console.log() s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory paradigm across all 17 supported clients, plus the OpenClaw gateway integration: stop treating the LLM as a data processor, treat it as a code generator. // Before: 47 × Read() = 700 KB. After: 1 × ctx_execute() = 3.6 KB. ctx_execute ( "javascript" , ` const files = fs.readdirSync('src').filter(f => f.endsWith('.ts')); files.forEach(f => console.log(f + ': ' + fs.readFileSync('src/'+f,'utf8').split('\\n').length + ' lines')); ` ) ;

Think in Code — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and console.log() s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory paradigm across all 17 supported clients, plus the OpenClaw gateway integration: stop treating the LLM as a data processor, treat it as a code generator.

// Before: 47 × Read() = 700 KB. After: 1 × ctx_execute() = 3.6 KB. ctx_execute ( "javascript" , ` const files = fs.readdirSync('src').filter(f => f.endsWith('.ts')); files.forEach(f => console.log(f + ': ' + fs.readFileSync('src/'+f,'utf8').split('\\n').length + ' lines')); ` ) ;

- No prose-style enforcement — context-mode keeps raw data out of context but never dictates how the model writes its final answer. Brevity, completeness, formatting — your model's call (or yours via your own CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md ). Aggressive brevity prompts have been shown to degrade coding/reasoning benchmarks ( Moonshot AI on kimi-k2.5 ) — the routing block stays focused on where data goes , not on how the model talks .

## Install

Platforms are grouped by install complexity. Hook-capable platforms get automatic routing enforcement. Non-hook platforms need a one-time routing file copy.

Prerequisites: Claude Code v1.0.33+ ( claude --version ). If /plugin is not recognized, update first: brew upgrade claude-code or npm update -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code .

Install:

/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode /plugin install context-mode@context-mode

Restart Claude Code (or run /reload-plugins ).

Verify:

/context-mode:ctx-doctor

All checks should show [x] . The doctor validates runtimes, hooks, FTS5, and plugin registration.

Routing: Automatic. The SessionStart hook injects routing instructions at runtime — no file is written to your project. The plugin registers all hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, PreCompact, SessionStart, Stop) and 11 MCP tools — six sandbox tools ( ctx_batch_execute , ctx_execute , ctx_execute_file , ctx_index , ctx_search , ctx_fetch_and_index ) plus five meta-tools ( ctx_stats , ctx_doctor , ctx_upgrade , ctx_purge , ctx_insight ).

> Note: Slash commands are a Claude Code plugin feature. On other platforms, type ctx stats , ctx doctor , ctx index , ctx search , ctx upgrade , or ctx insight in the chat — the model calls the MCP tool automatically. See Utility Commands .

Status line (optional): Claude Code's plugin manifest cannot declare a status line, so this is a one-time manual edit to ~/.claude/settings.json :

{ "statusLine" : { "type" : " command " , "command" : " context-mode statusline " } }

After saving, restart Claude Code. The bar shows $ saved this session · $ saved across sessions · % efficient so you can see savings accumulate in real time. The wiring is path-free — context-mode statusline resolves through the bundled CLI regardless of where the plugin cache lives.

claude mcp add context-mode -- npx -y context-mode

This gives you all 11 MCP tools without automatic routing. The model can still use them — it just won't be nudged to prefer them over raw Bash/Read/WebFetch. Good for trying it out before committing to the full plugin.

# Spec Guardian

Let formal specs test AI implementations.

A FizzBee spec describes the state transitions your system allows. However, the spec does not test whether your implementation follows those transitions. SpecGuardian turns FizzBee's results into tests that check whether your implementation reaches an allowed state.

SpecGuardian lets you verify that an AI-generated implementation actually conforms to your specification.

## From Spec to Test: Cache-Aside

In this cache-aside example, a WriteAndInvalidate action stores a new value in the database, then invalidates the corresponding cache entry. The tutorial spec models each operation as atomic and allows a crash before or between them:

@ conformance role CacheAside : fair action WriteAndInvalidate : # Yield to allow a crash before the first I/O. atomic : pass # Write to the database first, then invalidate the cache. db . write ( self . key , self . write_value ) cache . delete_cache ( self . key )

SpecGuardian generates Go tests from FizzBee's results. They compare the observed state after the action with states allowed by the spec, including states reached when an I/O operation fails.

For example, the generated Go test injects an error into the implementation just before cache invalidation, then checks whether the resulting state is allowed by the spec.

### Catching a Spec Mismatch

Consider an ordering bug in WriteAndInvalidate : cache invalidation runs before the database write.

func (ca *CacheAside) WriteAndInvalidate(ctx context.Context, input *Input) (*Output, error) { + if err := ca.cache.Delete(ctx, input.Key); err != nil { + return nil, err + } + if err := ca.db.Write(ctx, input.Key, input.Value); err != nil { return nil, err } - if err := ca.cache.Delete(ctx, input.Key); err != nil { - return nil, err - } - return &Output{Key: input.Key, Value: input.Value}, nil }

Both orders produce the same final state on success. But when the database write fails after cache invalidation, the database still holds old value and the cache entry is gone. The spec writes to the database first, so stopping at any point cannot produce this combination.

The test fails with the following output (excerpt):

actual state does not match any allowed state: I/O events: 1. valkey.Do 2. sql.BeginTx [fault injected; call not executed]

The mismatch excerpts show the unchanged database value and missing cache entry:

Fields.DB.Records[0].Value (-want +got): string( - "new", + "old", )

Fields.Cache.CachedRecords (-want +got): map[string]string{ - "cached": "old", }

## Getting Started

To try this example locally, start with the included cache-aside write tutorial. You'll need Go and Docker Compose; the FizzBee exploration results and generated tests are included.

Clone the repository and run the example:

git clone https://github.com/mrasu/spec-guardian.git cd spec-guardian/examples/tutorial_cache_aside_write docker compose up -d go test -count=1 -tags=specguardian ./conformance/...

The test passes, checking normal completion and injected I/O failures. Apply the diff above to cache_aside.go and rerun the go test command to reproduce the failure. Restore the original order to make the test pass again.

## How It Works

Here's how SpecGuardian works:

- FizzBee explores the possible states described by the spec.

- SpecGuardian generates Go tests from the exploration results.

- Either AI or you write the setup and Action execution code, configure providers in specguardian.yml , and write any remaining state observation code.

- The tests run a function normally and with an error injected immediately before a supported I/O call, then compare the observed state with states allowed by the spec.

specguardian.yml configures state observation and comparison. See the configuration schema for available settings and the example configuration for an example.

## When to Use

SpecGuardian checks whether an Action ends in a state allowed by the FizzBee spec, including after an injected I/O failure. It complements other tests:

- Different from unit tests: It checks the resulting application state against the spec, beyond assertions about individual functions.

- Different from integration tests: The expected states come from a FizzBee spec defined independently of the implementation.

## Generate Tests for Your Project

To generate tests for your project, install FizzBee and run these commands from your Go module directory:

fizz --output-dir path/to/output_dir path/to/YourSpec.fizz go get -tool github.com/mrasu/spec-guardian go tool spec-guardian init --fizzbee-output-dir path/to/output_dir # Configure observation and comparison. $EDITOR specguardian.yml go generate ./conformance # Replace <role> with the generated role name and connect the tests to your application. $EDITOR " conformance/specguardian/<role>_conformance_impl_test.go " go mod tidy go test -tags=specguardian ./conformance/...

See the user guide for the complete setup.

## Examples

- Cache-aside write tutorial is the completed project from the user guide .

- Cache-aside demonstrates the cache-aside pattern.

- Idempotent request demonstrates idempotent requests.

- Iceberg is a real-world example that tests apache/iceberg-go .

## Current Scope

SpecGuardian currently generates Go tests for one FizzBee Action invocation at a time. See the guardian directory for the available I/O hooks.

SpecGuardian is under development. Its public APIs or generated Go code may change.

# linkedin-ops

High-reliability, multi-agent-safe LinkedIn automation engine and CLI built on Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP).

> Disclaimer & Responsible Use : linkedin-ops is an independent open-source tool built for developer automation research, testing, and workflow automation via local Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by LinkedIn Corporation. Automated interaction with LinkedIn must comply with applicable platform terms and policies. Always maintain realistic human delays and respect LinkedIn rate limits to safeguard account health.

## Quickstart (<30s Setup)

### 1. Install dependencies

npm install

### 2. Run automated setup

node index.mjs setup

The setup wizard automatically:

- Locates your Google Chrome binary (macOS, Linux, Windows).

- Discovers your existing Chrome profiles from system User Data so you can pick your logged-in account (or create a dedicated project session).

- Saves settings to .linkedin-opsrc (no manual path pasting required).

- Generates a one-click launcher ( start-chrome.command / start-chrome.bat ).

### 3. Verify session & connection

npm run doctor # or: node index.mjs doctor

Checks CDP port 9222 reachability, browser version, user agent, and verifies an authenticated LinkedIn session.

### 4. Run your first dry run

node index.mjs connect --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --note= " Hi, loved your post on distributed systems... "

(Dry-run mode navigates and fills the note without submitting. Add --send only when ready to live submit).

## Architecture Guarantees

- Automated Runtime Fallback : Daily commands ping port 9222. If Chrome is closed, linkedin-ops automatically launches it using your configured profile. If Chrome is already running without remote debugging enabled, it detects the profile lock and prompts to restart cleanly.

- Cross-Process Mutex Locking : Serializes execution across concurrent agents and processes ( linkedin.lock ). Prevents session collisions, focus-stealing, and rate-limiting.

- Isolated Ephemeral Tabs : Each operation spawns its own dedicated Chrome tab via PUT /json/new and connects directly via target ID.

- Auto-Cleanup : Guarantees tab destruction ( /json/close/<targetId> ) in a finally block on success or failure, eliminating zombie tab leaks.

## CLI Usage

# Automated setup wizard node index.mjs setup # Pre-flight health check node index.mjs doctor # Connection invitation with personalized note (dry-run) node index.mjs connect --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --note= " Hi, loved your post... " # Live connection invitation node index.mjs connect --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --note= " Hi, loved your post... " --send # Direct message to 1st-degree connection node index.mjs dm --profile= " https://www.linkedin.com/in/username " --message= " Checking in on our conversation. " --send # Comment on a LinkedIn post node index.mjs comment --url= " https://www.linkedin.com/posts/... " --text= " Great insights on distributed systems! " --send # Company people search (e.g. recruiters) node index.mjs search --company= " Google " --keywords= " recruiter " --limit=10 --json # Inspect or force-release active mutex lock node index.mjs lock node index.mjs lock release

## Programmatic Library Usage

import { withLock , withDedicatedTab , sendConnectionInvite } from 'linkedin-ops' ; await withLock ( 'outreach-task' , async ( ) => { await withDedicatedTab ( { port : 9222 } , async ( cdp ) => { const result = await sendConnectionInvite ( cdp , { linkedinUrl : 'https://www.linkedin.com/in/username' , note : 'Hi, loved your work on distributed systems.' , send : true } ) ; console . log ( result ) ; } ) ; } ) ;

## Batch Campaigns

For multi-profile outreach and candidate sweeps, see campaigns/batch-connect.example.mjs :

# Copy template to your personal user campaigns folder cp campaigns/batch-connect.example.mjs campaigns/my-outreach.mjs # Run the campaign safely with mutex locking and isolated tab lifecycles node campaigns/my-outreach.mjs

(User campaigns and harvested datasets in data/ and campaigns/ are gitignored and never committed to source control).

## Documentation

- DATA_CONTRACT.md : Strict definition of the System Layer vs User Layer boundaries.

- Architecture Blueprint : Deep dive into CDP socket lifecycle, locking mechanisms, and tab management.
